quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Focus on the last sound of "that". With a bilabial consonant starting "meal" right after it, what shift would make pronunciation easier?
quests.explanation: Rather than jump from the /t/ ending "that" to a bilabial sound, the mouth compromises: /t/ becomes /p/, matching the bilabial consonant that opens "meal".
quests.phoneticRule: Unlike elision, assimilation keeps the sound but reshapes it. /t/, /d/, and /n/ typically shift toward /p, b, m, k/ or /g/ when one of those sounds follows.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Check the spelling of "you" before "and" — does it end in a letter that would predict a /w/ sound? If not, where's that /w/ actually coming from?
quests.explanation: Unlike linking, where the connecting sound is already written into the word, this /w/ in "you and" comes from nowhere in the spelling. That's exactly what makes it intrusive rather than a genuine linking sound.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "ten minutes" quickly, the way you'd say it in conversation. Which consonant do you actually hear where /n/ used to be?
quests.explanation: In fluent speech, /n/ rarely stays /n/ before a bilabial sound — it assimilates to /m/, which is exactly what you hear in "ten minutes".
quests.phoneticRule: Alveolar consonants like /t/, /d/, and /n/ often shift to match the place of articulation of a following bilabial (/p, b, m/) or velar (/k, g/) sound.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "most of them" at a natural conversational pace. Does "of" keep its full vowel sound, or shrink to a quick "uh"?
quests.explanation: Unstressed function words like "of" almost always reduce their vowel to schwa /ə/ in connected speech. Its full form is /ɒ/, but in "most of them" it shrinks to something much quicker and quieter.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "September and" naturally. That final 'r' in "September", usually silent, resurfaces here — why, do you think?
quests.explanation: This is linking, not intrusion, because the 'r' is already written into "September". It stays silent before a pause or consonant but comes back to life right before the vowel that opens "and".
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "him" isn't the stressed word in "him and her". What usually happens to an unstressed function word's vowel in fast speech?
quests.explanation: This is a weak form: "him" keeps its full vowel /æ/ only when stressed or said alone. In natural speech like "him and her", it reduces to schwa because it carries no sentence stress.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Try stressing every word in "she was tired" equally — it sounds stiff and unnatural, right? Which word loses its full vowel to fix that?
quests.explanation: English sentence rhythm relies on this kind of reduction — content words stay strong, function words like "was" go weak. That's why /ɒ/ becomes schwa in "she was tired".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Vowel sounds rarely bump directly into each other in fluent English. What extra sound bridges "area" and "around" here?
quests.explanation: Two vowel sounds meeting head-on is hard to say smoothly, so speakers add /r/ as a natural bridge. You'll hear it in "area around", even though neither word's spelling contains it.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Function words like "that" rarely keep their dictionary pronunciation in natural sentences. Listen for what its vowel becomes in "the book that I read".
quests.explanation: Because "that" isn't emphasized in "the book that I read", its vowel weakens from the full /æ/ to a fast, neutral schwa sound. This happens to almost every unstressed function word in fluent English.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In "she can swim", one word carries no stress at all. Focus on "can" — what happens to its vowel as a result?
quests.explanation: Weak forms like this one are what make native speech sound smooth rather than choppy. "can" trades its citation vowel /æ/ for schwa whenever it's unstressed, as it is in "she can swim".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant collision at the boundary of "about" and "your": /t/ meets /j/. Which single sound comes out the other side?
quests.explanation: Coalescence happens when neighboring sounds are so close in the mouth that they collapse into one. /t/ and /j/ become /tʃ/ in "about your" — faster and easier to say than keeping the two sounds apart.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen to the boundary between "set" and "off". A consonant and a vowel are meeting — what does fluent speech do with them?
quests.explanation: Rather than pausing between the consonant and the vowel, speakers connect them directly — the consonant essentially becomes the first sound of the next syllable. You hear this clearly in "set off".
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "search for answers" quickly, the way you would in real conversation. Does "for" sound the same as when you say it alone?
quests.explanation: Say "for" on its own and you get the full vowel /ɔː/. Say it inside "search for answers" at natural speed, and it reduces to schwa — the standard weak form.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "do" said by itself has a full, clear vowel. Said inside "what do you think" at natural speed, does that vowel survive?
quests.explanation: This reduction isn't sloppy speech — it's a predictable, rule-governed feature of English. Unstressed "do" reduces from /uː/ to schwa in virtually every natural sentence, including "what do you think".
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: In natural speech, a word-final consonant followed by a vowel often gets pulled into the next syllable. Does that happen between "turn" and "it"?
quests.explanation: This smooth consonant-to-vowel connection is what makes native speech sound joined-up rather than word-by-word. "turn it" links this way naturally.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: A stop consonant squeezed between two other consonants rarely survives in fast speech. Listen for the /t/ in "looked tired" — is it there?
quests.explanation: Consonant clusters like this one are common at word boundaries in English, and the middle stop is almost always the casualty. The /t/ drops out of "looked tired" for exactly that reason.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision deletes a sound completely rather than changing it. It happens most often to /t/ and /d/ when they're trapped between two other consonants.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "drop" ends in a consonant; "off" begins with a vowel. Try saying them together quickly — which word does that consonant sound like it belongs to now?
quests.explanation: No sound is created or lost here — the final consonant of "drop" simply carries over to open the vowel in "off", which is the essence of linking in connected speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Content words — nouns, verbs, adjectives — usually keep their full vowels; function words like "and" often don't. What happens to it in "rock and roll"?
quests.explanation: Stress timing in English means unstressed words get compressed. "and" loses its full /æ/ vowel and reduces to schwa here, keeping "rock and roll" flowing at a natural rhythm.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a classic resyllabification moment. What happens to the last sound of "take" once the vowel of "off" is right there waiting?
quests.explanation: Because a vowel immediately follows, the closing consonant of "take" doesn't stay put — it links forward into "off", exactly as fluent speakers naturally do.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final consonant, or a normally-silent final 'r', reattaches to a following vowel sound, joining the two words into one smooth unit.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen for the schwa. Somewhere in "plan to travel", a full vowel gets flattened into that quick, neutral "uh" sound — which word is it?
quests.explanation: Native listeners expect this weak form; a fully stressed /uː/ on "to" in "plan to travel" would actually sound unnatural or overly formal. The relaxed schwa is the normal, expected pronunciation.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Check the spelling: "order" ends in 'r'. Before a consonant or pause it usually stays silent — so what happens before the vowel starting "online"?
quests.explanation: The final 'r' in "order" behaves like a switch: silent before consonants, audible before vowels. Since "online" starts with a vowel, the /r/ links the two words together smoothly.
quests.phoneticRule: Linking happens when a sound already present — in pronunciation or in spelling — carries across a word boundary onto a following vowel, unlike intrusion, where the sound has no spelling basis at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: "was" is grammatically necessary but rarely emphasized. What does that lack of stress do to its vowel in "it was fun"?
quests.explanation: This is one of the most common patterns in spoken English: function words reduce, content words don't. "was" follows that rule exactly, shrinking from /ɒ/ to schwa in "it was fun".
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed grammatical words shrink to their weak form, trading a full vowel for schwa — this is one of the most frequent patterns in fluent English.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "burnt toast" quickly. The consonants pile up right around the /t/ in "burnt" — does it survive the crowd, or get squeezed out?
quests.explanation: When /t/ sits between two other consonants, English speakers routinely drop it to keep the rhythm smooth. In "burnt toast", the /t/ disappears rather than being pronounced.
quests.phoneticRule: When a stop consonant like /t/ or /d/ is sandwiched between two other consonants, English speakers usually drop it rather than force all three sounds together.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Say "a pair of shoes" at a natural conversational pace. Does "a" keep its full vowel sound, or shrink to a quick "uh"?
quests.explanation: Unstressed function words like "a" almost always reduce their vowel to schwa /ə/ in connected speech. Its full form is /ɒ/, but in "a pair of shoes" it shrinks to something much quicker and quieter.
quests.phoneticRule: Function words like "a", "to", "of", "was", and "can" reduce their vowel to a quick schwa /ə/ whenever they're unstressed, which is almost always in natural speech.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's no /w/ anywhere in the spelling of "you". Yet something links it to the vowel that opens "ought" — what is it?
quests.explanation: This inserted /w/ has no basis in spelling — it exists purely to smooth the vowel-to-vowel transition between "you" and "ought". That's the hallmark of intrusion.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Two consonants become one here. Focus on where "support" ends and "your" begins — what's the resulting blended sound?
quests.explanation: This merge is extremely common wherever a word ending in /t/ meets a "you"-type word. In "support your", the result is /tʃ/, not /t/ followed by /j/.
quests.phoneticRule: When /t/, /d/, /s/, or /z/ meets /j/ across a word boundary, the two sounds often fuse into a brand-new consonant: /tʃ/, /dʒ/, /ʃ/, or /ʒ/.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Listen carefully between "essay" and "about". An unwritten sound appears purely to ease the vowel-to-vowel transition. Which one?
quests.explanation: Native speakers automatically fill the gap between two vowel sounds with /j/, even when there's no letter to justify it. "essay about" is a clear example of this intrusive sound.
quests.phoneticRule: English avoids two vowel sounds colliding directly, so an extra /r/, /w/, or /j/ sound is inserted between them — even though that sound doesn't appear in either word's spelling.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: Rather than pronouncing /z/ then /j/ separately, fluent speakers coalesce them. What do you actually hear in "use your"?
quests.explanation: Notice that neither the original /z/ nor /j/ survives on its own — they combine into /ʒ/. That fusion is what makes "use your" sound natural and fast.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescent assimilation merges two adjacent sounds into a completely different third sound — most often where a word ending in /t, d, s/, or /z/ meets a "y"-initial word like "you" or "your".

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: There's a consonant cluster forming between "just" and "married". In natural speech, one sound in that cluster usually disappears. Which one?
quests.explanation: Three consonants in a row are hard to articulate cleanly, so speakers simplify by deleting the middle one. That's exactly what happens to the /t/ in "just married" — it's dropped, not just softened.
quests.phoneticRule: In consonant clusters, /t/ and /d/ are the sounds most likely to disappear entirely — this is called elision, and it keeps fast speech from sounding choppy.

quests.instruction: IDENTIFY THE CONNECTED SPEECH PHENOMENON IN THE PHRASE
quests.hint: This is a spelling trap: "away" looks like it should flow straight into "at", but a sound gets inserted that isn't written anywhere. Can you hear it?
quests.explanation: Since "away" doesn't end in a written consonant that could explain a /j/, the /j/ you hear before "at" is added by the speech system itself — an intrusive sound, not a spelled one.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive sounds (/r/, /w/, /j/) bridge vowel-to-vowel gaps in connected speech purely for smoothness, with no basis in spelling at all.
